modules.title: Professional Cooking Techniques
modules.overview: Professional cooks get the same result every time because they understand what heat, water, fat and time do to food. This module teaches four core methods: making stock and sauces, braising tough cuts, roasting and grilling with dry heat, and frying safely. Each lesson gives you the reason behind the method, a worked example with real quantities, and the safety rules a professional kitchen follows.

lessons.title: Stocks, reductions and sauces: building flavour from bones
objectives: Make a clear chicken or beef stock using the correct ratio, heat and timing
Cool, label and store stock safely
Thicken a sauce with a roux or by reduction and predict the final volume
Name the five classic mother sauces and one local use for each method

blocks.text: Many home cooks in Nigeria build flavour with seasoning cubes. They are quick, but they add a lot of salt and every pot ends up tasting the same. Professional kitchens build flavour from **stock**: water that has been slowly simmered with bones, a few vegetables and herbs. A good stock gives body to soups, stews, rice and sauces, and it lets you control exactly how much salt goes into the food.

blocks.name: pot-of-food
blocks.caption: A stockpot kept at a gentle simmer is the base of most professional sauces and soups.

blocks.text: What makes a good stock

items: **Bones with connective tissue.** Chicken backs, necks, wings and feet, or beef knuckle and leg bones. The connective tissue melts into gelatin, which gives the stock body. A well-made chicken stock sets like soft jelly in the fridge.
**Cold water to start.** Put the bones in cold water so that proteins rise slowly as foam and can be skimmed off. Use enough water to cover the bones by about 5 cm.
**Aromatics.** About one part vegetables to ten parts bones by weight is the classic guide. Locally that can be onion, garlic, ginger, a few thyme stems and bay leaves.
**A gentle simmer, never a hard boil.** Small bubbles should just break the surface. Hard boiling churns fat into the liquid and makes stock cloudy and greasy.
**No salt.** Stock is often reduced later. Salt added now becomes too strong after reduction. Season the final dish instead.

head: Stock
Bones prepared by
Usual simmer time
Best used in
rows: Rinsing heads and frames, gills removed

blocks.text: Fish stock is short because fish bones are thin and turn bitter if cooked too long. Beef bones are dense and need hours to give up their gelatin. These times are the usual range in professional training, not strict rules.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 3-litre chicken stock and what it costs
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma runs a small lunch kitchen in Enugu and wants to replace seasoning cubes in her pepper soup with homemade stock.
steps: She buys 2 kg of chicken backs, necks and feet. She rinses them, covers them with 4 litres of cold water and brings the pot slowly to a simmer.
She skims the grey foam for the first 20 minutes, then adds 200 g of aromatics (onion, garlic, ginger and thyme). That is 10% of the bone weight.
She keeps it barely simmering for 3 hours, skimming fat now and then. About a quarter of the water evaporates, so she strains out roughly 3 litres.
Her costs (approximate, prices change often): bones about N5,000, aromatics about N1,000, gas about N800. Total about N6,800.
Cost per litre: N6,800 divided by 3 = about N2,267. A 1-litre pot of pepper soup now carries about N2,267 of stock instead of cubes, and she controls the salt.
blocks.result: Ifeoma has a stock with real body and no added salt. She labels it with the date and uses it within 3 days from the fridge, or freezes it in 500 ml bags.

blocks.title: Making stock the professional way
items: Rinse or roast bones
Cover with cold water
Simmer gently and skim
Strain and cool fast
Label, chill or freeze
blocks.caption: Each step protects clarity, flavour and safety, from raw bones to stored stock.

blocks.title: Cool stock quickly
blocks.text: A big hot pot cools very slowly, and bacteria grow fastest between about 5 C and 60 C. Divide stock into shallow containers, stand them in a basin of cold water with ice if you have it, and refrigerate within 2 hours. Never leave stock on the stove overnight to cool.
Reduction: concentrating flavour

**Reduction** means simmering a liquid uncovered so water evaporates and the flavour concentrates. If you reduce 1 litre of stock to 250 ml, you have removed three quarters of the water and the flavour is about four times as strong. A stock reduced until it coats the back of a spoon is called a **glaze**. A spoonful of glaze gives a stew or gravy a deep, rounded taste without adding salt.
Thickening with a roux

A **roux** is equal weights of fat and flour cooked together before liquid is added. Cooking the flour removes its raw taste. A pale roux (cooked 2 to 3 minutes) thickens strongly. A brown roux has a nutty flavour but less thickening power. As a guide, about 40 to 50 g each of butter and flour thickens 500 to 600 ml of milk to a medium sauce. Add warm liquid gradually and whisk to prevent lumps, then simmer for a few minutes so the flour finishes cooking.
The five mother sauces

French cooking groups classic sauces into five **mother sauces**: béchamel (milk thickened with roux), velouté (light stock thickened with roux), espagnole (brown stock with roux and tomato), tomato sauce, and hollandaise (egg yolks and melted butter). You do not need French dishes to use the ideas. Velouté made with chicken stock becomes a white sauce for chicken pies. A reduced brown stock improves your beef stew gravy. The principle is the same: good stock plus a controlled way of thickening.

blocks.title: Taste at the end
blocks.text: Season sauces only after reducing and thickening. Taste, add a little salt, stir, taste again. It is easy to add salt and impossible to take it out.

takeaways: Start bones in cold water, simmer gently, skim, and never salt the stock
Aromatics are about 10% of the bone weight
Reducing 1 litre to 250 ml makes flavour about four times stronger
A roux is equal weights of fat and flour, cooked before adding liquid
Cool stock in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours

activity.title: Make, cost and store one stock
steps: Buy 1 to 2 kg of chicken or beef bones and weigh out aromatics at 10% of the bone weight.
Make the stock, writing down start time, water volume and when you skimmed.
Strain and measure how much stock you got, then calculate the cost per litre.
Cool it in shallow containers and label each with the date.
Reduce 500 ml to about 125 ml and taste the difference.
activity.evidence: A photo of your labelled stock containers and a note of the cost per litre

lessons.title: Braising and slow cooking tough cuts until tender
objectives: Explain why tough cuts become tender with long, moist, gentle heat
Braise goat meat, cow leg or oxtail using sear, liquid and low simmer
Use a pressure cooker safely to shorten braising time
Check doneness by texture rather than by the clock

blocks.text: Goat meat, cow leg, shin, oxtail and old layer chicken are full of flavour but tough. They come from muscles that worked hard, so they contain a lot of **collagen**, the connective tissue that holds muscle fibres together. Quick, hot cooking makes collagen tighten and the meat goes rubbery. Long, gentle, moist heat does the opposite: collagen slowly melts into gelatin and the meat becomes soft enough to pull apart with a fork.

blocks.name: cut-of-meat
blocks.caption: Hard-working cuts such as shin and oxtail are rich in collagen, which braising turns to tender gelatin.

blocks.text: What braising means

**Braising** is searing meat in a little fat, then cooking it slowly in a covered pot with liquid that comes part of the way up the meat, usually about half to two thirds. **Stewing** is similar, but the pieces are smaller and fully covered with liquid. Both rely on the same science. The liquid stays at a low simmer, well below a rolling boil, for a long time.

items: **Dry and season the meat.** Pat it dry with a clean cloth or paper. Wet meat steams instead of browning.
**Sear in batches.** Brown the pieces in a little hot oil without crowding the pot. Browning creates new flavour compounds on the surface.
**Soften aromatics.** Cook onions, garlic, ginger and pepper in the same pot to pick up the browned bits.
**Deglaze and add liquid.** Pour in stock or water and scrape the bottom of the pot. Add liquid until it reaches about half to two thirds of the meat.
**Cover and cook low.** Keep a lazy simmer with only occasional bubbles. Turn the meat once or twice.
**Finish the sauce.** When the meat is tender, lift it out and reduce the liquid until it is glossy and coats a spoon.

head: Cut
Typical gentle braise on the stove
Signs it is ready
rows: Meat pulls from the bone easily
Skin and tendon are soft and sticky
Meat slides off the joint with a fork
Thigh meat is soft, not springy

blocks.text: These times vary with the age of the animal, the size of the pieces and how steady your heat is. Always judge by texture. A fork should slide in with little resistance.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a goat meat braise for a Sunday lunch
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano is cooking 3 kg of goat meat for a family lunch of 12 and wants the meat soft by 1:00 pm.
steps: She plans 250 g of raw meat with bone per person: 3,000 g divided by 250 g = 12 portions.
She allows 30 minutes to sear in three batches of 1 kg, so the pot is never crowded.
She adds 1.5 litres of stock, which comes about two thirds of the way up the meat in her 10-litre pot.
Her goat usually needs about 2 hours at a low simmer, and she adds 30 minutes for reducing the sauce and a 30-minute safety margin.
Working backwards from 1:00 pm: 1:00 minus 30 minutes margin, minus 30 minutes reducing, minus 2 hours braising, minus 30 minutes searing = 9:30 am start.
blocks.result: Halima starts searing at 9:30 am. If the meat is ready early, she holds it hot in the covered pot, above 60 C, rather than letting it cool.

blocks.title: Halima's braise, worked backwards
items: 9:30 Sear in batches
10:00 Add liquid, cover
12:00 Tender, reduce sauce
12:30 Margin, hold hot
1:00 Serve
blocks.caption: Planning backwards from serving time removes last-minute rushing.

blocks.text: Pressure cookers: faster, but respect them

A pressure cooker traps steam, which raises the boiling point of the water inside to roughly 115 to 120 C. Collagen melts much faster at that temperature, so a cow leg that needs 3 hours on an open stove may be ready in well under an hour. Follow the time chart in your cooker's manual, because models differ.

blocks.title: Pressure cooker rules
blocks.text: Never fill above the maximum line, usually two thirds full, or half full for beans and foods that foam. Check that the vent and gasket are clean before every use. Never force the lid open: let the pressure drop naturally or use the release method in the manual, keeping your face and hands away from the steam. Replace a cracked or hardened gasket.
Why braised dishes taste better the next day

As a braise rests, gelatin sets and flavours spread through the meat. Many caterers braise a day ahead. If you do, cool it quickly in shallow trays, refrigerate within 2 hours, lift off the hardened fat the next day, and reheat until it is steaming hot all the way through, at least 70 C in the thickest piece.

blocks.title: Do not boil it hard
blocks.text: A hard boil squeezes moisture out of the muscle fibres and gives dry, stringy meat even when the collagen has melted. Keep the bubbles lazy.

takeaways: Tough cuts are rich in collagen, which melts into gelatin with long, gentle, moist heat
Sear dry meat in batches, then braise in liquid about half to two thirds up the meat
Judge doneness by texture, not the clock
Pressure cookers are fast but must never be overfilled or forced open
Plan cooking backwards from serving time and include a safety margin

activity.title: Braise and time one tough cut
steps: Choose a cut: goat meat, cow leg, shin or oxtail, and weigh it.
Write a backwards timetable from your serving time, including searing and reducing.
Braise it, checking texture every 30 minutes after the first hour.
Record the actual time it took and how the sauce looked after reducing.
activity.evidence: Your written timetable with the actual times added, and a photo of the finished dish

lessons.title: Roasting and grilling: browning, doneness and charcoal safety
objectives: Explain how dry heat browns food and why surface moisture stops it
Roast or grill chicken and fish to a safe internal temperature using a thermometer
Rest meat correctly and estimate cooking loss
Use charcoal and gas grills without smoke, fire or carbon monoxide danger

blocks.text: Roasting (in an oven) and grilling (over or under direct heat, like suya or asun) are **dry-heat** methods. Hot air or radiant heat dries the surface of the food and then browns it. That brown crust is where much of the flavour comes from, and it is the reason a well-grilled fish tastes so different from a boiled one.

blocks.name: poultry-leg
blocks.caption: A deep brown surface comes from browning reactions, which need a dry surface and high heat.

blocks.text: The science of browning

When the surface of meat, fish or bread gets hot enough, sugars and proteins react to form hundreds of new flavour and colour compounds. This is called the **Maillard reaction**. It happens quickly above about 140 C. Water boils at 100 C, so a wet surface cannot get hotter than that until the water has gone. That is why professionals pat meat dry, salt it ahead so the surface dries, and never crowd a tray. Crowded pieces release steam and end up grey instead of brown.

items: **Dry the surface.** Pat chicken and fish dry before seasoning and oiling.
**Leave space.** Keep at least a finger's width between pieces on a tray or grill.
**Use high heat to brown, moderate heat to finish.** Thick pieces need time to cook through without burning outside.
**Add sugary marinades late.** Honey, sugar or sweet sauces burn quickly; brush them on in the last few minutes.

blocks.text: In a home or bakery oven, many cooks roast chicken pieces at about 190 to 200 C. Oven dials are often inaccurate, so an oven thermometer placed on the middle shelf tells you the real temperature. Turn the tray halfway through, because most ovens are hotter at the back.
Cooked through, not guessed

The only reliable way to know chicken is safely cooked is to measure the temperature in the thickest part, away from the bone. The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food advise cooking food until it reaches 70 C. A digital probe thermometer costs far less than one case of food poisoning at an event. Clear juices and no pink colour are helpful signs but they are not proof.

Check
Safe sign
rows: Probe the thickest thigh, not touching bone
At least 70 C, juices run clear
Probe the centre of the thickest piece
At least 70 C, flesh opaque and firm
Flesh opaque and flakes easily, at least 70 C
At least 70 C, no pink inside

blocks.text: Resting and cooking loss

Meat loses water as it cooks, so it weighs less afterwards. This **cooking loss** matters when you are buying for a crowd. Rest meat for 5 to 10 minutes after roasting so juices settle back into the fibres instead of running onto the board. Keep it loosely covered and warm.

blocks.title: Worked example: measuring cooking loss on grilled chicken
blocks.context: For example, Chinwe in Port Harcourt sells grilled chicken quarters and wants to know how much raw chicken to buy for 40 servings of 200 g cooked meat.
steps: She weighs 2,000 g of raw chicken quarters before grilling.
After grilling and resting, the same pieces weigh 1,500 g.
Cooking loss = 2,000 minus 1,500 = 500 g. As a percentage: 500 divided by 2,000 = 25%.
So cooked weight is 75% of raw weight. To get 40 x 200 g = 8,000 g cooked, she needs 8,000 divided by 0.75 = about 10,667 g raw.
She rounds up to 11 kg of raw chicken quarters.
blocks.result: Chinwe buys 11 kg instead of guessing 8 kg, so every customer gets a full 200 g portion. She repeats the test whenever she changes supplier, because the loss changes with the size and fat of the birds.

blocks.title: Grilling chicken quarters well
items: Pat dry and season
Brown over high heat
Move to moderate heat
Probe: at least 70 C
Rest 5 to 10 minutes
blocks.caption: Brown first, finish gently, check with a thermometer, then rest before serving.

blocks.title: Charcoal and carbon monoxide
blocks.text: Burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Never use a charcoal grill or coal pot inside a room, kitchen, garage or tent, even with a window open. Grill outdoors, away from doors and windows, with a bucket of sand nearby. Never pour kerosene or petrol on burning coals.

blocks.title: Avoid heavy charring
blocks.text: Fat dripping onto hot coals creates smoke and flare-ups that blacken the food. Food safety agencies advise limiting heavily charred and burnt meat. Trim excess fat, keep a cooler zone on the grill to move food to during flare-ups, and scrape off blackened bits.

Clean the grill grate while it is hot with a wire brush, then wipe it with an oiled cloth before the next use. Keep raw meat trays and cooked meat trays separate, and never put cooked suya back on the plate that held it raw.

takeaways: Browning (the Maillard reaction) needs a dry surface and high heat
Use a probe thermometer: chicken and fish should reach at least 70 C in the thickest part
Cooking loss is often around a quarter of raw weight, so measure it and buy accordingly
Rest roasted meat 5 to 10 minutes before cutting
Charcoal is for outdoors only because of carbon monoxide

activity.title: Run a cooking loss test
steps: Weigh a batch of raw chicken or fish and write the weight down.
Grill or roast it, checking the thickest piece with a thermometer.
Rest it, weigh it again and calculate the cooking loss percentage.
Work out how much raw meat you would need for 50 portions of 150 g cooked.
activity.evidence: A note showing raw weight, cooked weight, loss percentage and your 50-portion calculation

lessons.title: Deep frying and shallow frying: oil temperature, oil care and fire safety
objectives: Choose a frying oil and hold it at the right temperature
Fry plantain, fish or yam evenly without greasy or burnt results
Decide when frying oil must be filtered or thrown away
Respond correctly to an oil fire

blocks.text: Frying is one of the most common methods in Nigerian kitchens: dodo, fried yam, akara, fried fish, fried turkey. It is also where many kitchen burns and fires start. Good frying is about one thing above all: **oil temperature**. Oil that is too cool soaks into the food and makes it greasy. Oil that is too hot burns the outside before the inside cooks, and starts to smoke and break down.

blocks.name: shallow-pan-of-food
blocks.alt: A shallow pan with food frying
blocks.caption: Steady oil temperature is the difference between crisp, golden food and greasy or burnt food.

blocks.text: Deep frying and shallow frying

In **deep frying**, food is fully covered by oil, usually held at about 170 to 180 C. In **shallow frying**, the oil comes part way up the food and you turn it once, as with dodo or fish fillets. When cold food goes into hot oil, the water at its surface turns to steam and bubbles out. That outward steam is what stops oil soaking in. When the bubbling slows, the food is nearly done.

head: Food
Oil temperature guide
What to watch
rows: Sugars brown fast; turn once when golden
Fry until golden, not dark brown
Dry well first to reduce spitting
Drop batter gently; turn for even colour

blocks.text: A clip-on or probe thermometer is best. Without one, drop in a 2 cm cube of bread: at roughly the right temperature for most frying it turns golden in about 60 seconds with steady bubbles. If it browns in a few seconds, the oil is too hot. If it sinks and barely bubbles, it is too cool.
Choosing and caring for oil

items: **Use a stable oil for deep frying.** Refined vegetable oil, groundnut oil and refined palm olein handle frying heat well. Unrefined oils and butter smoke at lower temperatures.
**Fry in small batches.** Too much food at once drops the temperature sharply and gives greasy results.
**Salt away from the oil.** Salt food after frying, over a tray, because salt falling into oil speeds up its breakdown.
**Filter after use.** Let oil cool fully, strain it through a fine sieve or cloth into a clean, dry container with a lid, and store it away from light.
**Know when to throw it away.** Discard oil that is dark, thick, smells sharp or fishy, foams heavily, or smokes at normal frying heat.

blocks.title: Golden, not dark brown
blocks.text: Starchy foods such as yam, potato and plantain form a substance called acrylamide when fried or roasted to a dark colour. Food safety agencies, including the UK Food Standards Agency, advise frying starchy foods to a golden yellow colour rather than dark brown. It also tastes better.

blocks.title: Worked example: is the oil still worth using?
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Abeokuta fries plantain and fish for a roadside lunch stand and wants to control oil cost without serving food fried in burnt oil.
steps: She starts the week with 5 litres of vegetable oil in her deep pot. Oil costs her about N3,000 per litre (approximate).
She fries plantain first each day and fish last, because fish flavours the oil. She strains the oil every evening.
Each day she tops up about 0.5 litre lost into the food. By day 4 she has added 2 litres.
On day 4 the oil is dark, foams when fish goes in and smokes at her usual setting. She discards it.
Weekly oil cost: (5 + 2) litres x N3,000 = N21,000. Over 4 days of about 80 plates a day (320 plates), that is about N66 of oil per plate.
blocks.result: Funke knows her oil cost per plate and has a clear rule for discarding oil. Frying plantain before fish keeps her oil usable longer.

blocks.title: Discard frying oil if
items: Dark brown or black
Thick and sticky
Smokes at normal heat
Foams heavily
Smells sharp or rancid
blocks.caption: Any one of these signs means the oil has broken down and should not be used again.

blocks.title: If oil catches fire
blocks.text: Never pour water on burning oil: it turns to steam instantly and throws flaming oil across the room. Turn off the gas if you can reach it safely. Slide a metal lid or a damp (not dripping) fire blanket over the pot and leave it covered until fully cool. Do not carry the pot. If the fire spreads, get everyone out and call for help. A dry powder or wet chemical fire extinguisher suitable for kitchen fires is a good investment for a food business.

Prevent fires before they start. Never fill a pot more than about one third with oil. Keep the handle turned inwards. Lower food in gently with a slotted spoon instead of dropping it. Keep children out of the frying area. Never leave hot oil unattended, even for a phone call.

takeaways: Most frying works best at about 160 to 180 C; use a thermometer or the bread cube test
Fry small batches so the temperature does not crash
Fry starchy foods golden, not dark brown
Strain oil after use and discard it when dark, thick, foaming, smoky or rancid
Never put water on an oil fire: cover it and turn off the heat

activity.title: Frying test and oil log
steps: Heat oil and check it with a thermometer or the bread cube test.
Fry one batch of plantain at the right temperature and one batch with oil that is too cool.
Compare colour, crispness and greasiness and photograph both.
Start an oil log: date, litres added, foods fried, condition at the end of the day.

quiz.q: Ada's chicken stock came out cloudy and greasy. What is the most likely cause?
options: She started the bones in cold water
She let it boil hard instead of simmering gently
quiz.explain: Hard boiling churns fat and proteins into the liquid. Stock should only simmer gently, with small bubbles breaking the surface.

quiz.q: Bola reduces 2 litres of stock to 500 ml. Roughly how much stronger is the flavour?
quiz.explain: 2,000 ml divided by 500 ml = 4. Three quarters of the water has gone, so the flavour is about four times as concentrated.

quiz.q: Which method best tenderises a cow leg?
options: Fast frying in very hot oil
Grilling over high heat for 10 minutes
quiz.explain: Cow leg is full of collagen. It needs long, gentle, moist heat so the collagen melts into gelatin.

quiz.q: Chinwe's 3 kg of raw fish weighs 2.4 kg after grilling. What is the cooking loss?
quiz.explain: Loss = 3.0 minus 2.4 = 0.6 kg. 0.6 divided by 3.0 = 0.20, so 20%.

quiz.q: Oil in Kemi's pot catches fire. What should she do?
options: Pour a cup of water on it
Turn off the gas and slide a lid or fire blanket over the pot
Fan the flames to cool them
quiz.explain: Water on burning oil causes a fireball, and carrying the pot spills burning oil. Cut the heat and smother the fire with a lid or fire blanket.

quiz.q: How should Halima check that grilled chicken thighs are safely cooked?
options: Cut one open and look for pink
Probe the thickest part away from the bone: at least 70 C
Press them and see if they are firm
quiz.explain: Only a thermometer is reliable. The WHO Five Keys advise cooking until food reaches 70 C.

modules.title: Nigerian and West African Cuisine at a Professional Standard
modules.overview: Customers pay for food that tastes the same every time and looks cared for. This module turns familiar dishes into standard recipes you can repeat at any quantity, teaches you to cook West African grains, legumes and proteins with precision, and shows you how to plate and present food the way hotels and good restaurants do.

lessons.title: Standard recipes for soups and stews that taste the same every time
objectives: Write a standard recipe card with yield, portion size and weights
Prepare a reduced tomato and pepper stew base that keeps and fries cleanly
Build flavour in layers in egusi, efo riro and other soups
Calculate the yield and cost per portion of a stew base

blocks.text: Ask ten Nigerian cooks how they make stew and you will get ten answers, most of them "a little of this, a little of that". That works at home. In a business it causes problems: Tuesday's stew is sweeter than Monday's, one batch is too peppery, and you never know your true cost. Professional kitchens solve this with a **standard recipe**: the same ingredients, the same weights, the same method, every time.

blocks.name: chef
blocks.alt: A chef preparing food in a kitchen
blocks.caption: A standard recipe card lets you, or anyone you train, cook the dish the same way every time.

blocks.text: What goes on a standard recipe card

items: **Name and yield:** for example, "Tomato stew base, yield 4 kg".
**Portion size:** for example, 120 g of stew per plate.
**Ingredients by weight,** not cups or "handfuls". A kitchen scale is the most important tool in this course.
**Method in numbered steps** with times and visual signs, such as "fry until oil rises to the top".
**Critical points:** the steps that make or break the dish, such as reducing the base before frying.
**Storage and holding:** how long it keeps chilled, and how to reheat it.

blocks.text: The stew base: reduce before you fry

Fresh tomatoes are mostly water, roughly 94%. If you blend them and pour them straight into hot oil, the oil spits, the stew takes a long time to fry and the result can taste sour and raw. Professionals first **boil down** the blended tomato, tatashe (red bell pepper), scotch bonnet and onion until much of the water has gone. Then they fry the thick paste in oil until the oil separates and rises to the top. That sign means the water has cooked out and the sour, raw taste has gone.

blocks.title: Worked example: yield and cost of a stew base
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Owerri prepares stew base on Mondays for her weekday rice orders and wants to know her cost per portion.
steps: She blends 5 kg tomatoes, 1 kg tatashe, 0.5 kg scotch bonnet and 1 kg onions. Total blended weight: 7.5 kg.
She boils it uncovered until it has halved, checking by weighing the pot (she knows the empty pot weight). Reduced weight: about 3.75 kg.
She fries it in 0.6 kg of vegetable oil with seasoning until the oil rises. She weighs the finished base: 4 kg.
Ingredient cost (approximate prices): tomatoes N12,000, tatashe N4,000, scotch bonnet N2,000, onions N2,500, oil N1,800, seasoning N700. Total N23,000.
At 120 g per plate: 4,000 g divided by 120 g = 33 portions. Cost per portion: N23,000 divided by 33 = about N697.
blocks.result: Ngozi now knows each plate carries about N697 of stew. She writes the weights on her recipe card so her assistant can repeat it exactly.

Boil down by half
Fry until oil rises
Add stock and protein
Taste, adjust, cool or hold
blocks.caption: Removing water first is the step that gives a sweet, clean, long-keeping stew.

blocks.text: Layering flavour in soups

In soups, flavour is built in layers, and the order matters. For **egusi**, many professional cooks fry the ground melon in palm oil with a little onion, or drop it in as small lumps of paste and leave it to set before stirring, depending on whether the customer wants a fried or lumpy style. Both work; what matters is that you choose one style, write it down and always do it the same way.

items: **Base layer:** stock from the meats you cooked first. This is where the deep savoury taste comes from.
**Fat and aromatics:** palm oil, onion, locust beans (iru) or crayfish, cooked until fragrant.
**Body:** egusi, ogbono, cocoyam paste or blended vegetables that thicken the soup.
**Fresh layer last:** leafy vegetables such as ugwu, spinach (efo) or bitter leaf go in near the end so they stay green and keep more of their vitamins.
**Final check:** taste for salt, heat and sourness, then adjust in small steps.

blocks.title: Bleaching palm oil
blocks.text: Some cooks heat palm oil until it turns pale ("bleaching") for dishes such as ayamase. This produces heavy smoke and breaks down the oil. If you do it, use a small quantity, keep the heat moderate, stay with the pot, open doors and windows, and never let the oil catch fire. Many professional cooks prefer to buy refined palm oil or use green pepper sauce styles that do not need it.

blocks.title: Season in stages
blocks.text: Salt and seasoning cubes concentrate as soups reduce. Season lightly at the start, then adjust at the end. Write your final quantities on the recipe card.

Cooled stew base keeps well in a clean, covered container in the fridge for a few days, and much longer frozen in portion bags. Label each bag with the name, weight and date. Reheat only what you need, and bring it to a full simmer before serving.

takeaways: A standard recipe gives the same taste, portion and cost every time
Weigh ingredients; a kitchen scale is essential
Boil down blended tomatoes and peppers before frying; fry until the oil rises
Add leafy vegetables last to keep colour and vitamins
Know your cost per portion from your recipe card

activity.title: Write and test your first standard recipe
steps: Choose your best-selling soup or stew.
Cook it once, weighing every ingredient and timing every step.
Weigh the finished batch and decide a portion size.
Calculate the number of portions and the cost per portion.
Write it on a recipe card and ask someone else to cook it from the card.
activity.evidence: Your completed recipe card and a photo of the dish cooked by the second person

lessons.title: Cooking rice, acha, beans and proteins with precision
objectives: Cook parboiled rice, ofada and acha (fonio) to the right texture using measured water
Soak and cook beans to save fuel and improve digestibility
Combine grains and legumes for better quality protein
Buy and store grains and beans safely

blocks.text: Grains and legumes are the backbone of West African meals: rice, maize, millet, sorghum, acha (fonio), beans, soybeans and groundnuts. Cooking them well is a precision skill. Too much water gives mushy rice; too little gives hard grains and a burnt pot. In a business, the same mistake repeated over 100 portions is expensive.

blocks.name: beans
blocks.caption: Beans and grains cook best when you measure water and soak or wash them correctly.

blocks.text: Rice and acha: measure the water

For white rice cooked by the **absorption method**, you add just enough water for the grains to soak up, cover the pot and cook gently until the water is gone. Parboiled long-grain rice, the type most sold in Nigeria, usually needs more water than raw white rice because the grain is harder. Washing rice until the water runs nearly clear removes surface starch and helps stop grains sticking. Ofada rice is often a little stony, so pick it over carefully before washing.

head: Grain
Typical water by volume
What to watch
rows: About 1.5 to 2 cups water per cup rice
Brand and age change the amount; test once and record it
About 2 to 2.5 cups water per cup rice
Pick out stones; aroma is part of its appeal
About 2 cups water per cup acha
Cooks fast, in minutes; stir gently with a fork
About 3 cups water per cup grain
Longer cooking; can be soaked first

blocks.text: These are starting ratios. The right answer for your rice and your pot is the one you have tested and written down. When you scale up for a big pot, the water ratio stays roughly the same but less water evaporates per cup of rice, so reduce slightly and check.
Beans: soak, discard water, cook

items: **Sort.** Remove stones, damaged and insect-holed beans.
**Soak.** Cover with plenty of water and soak for 6 to 8 hours or overnight. Soaked beans cook noticeably faster, which saves gas.
**Discard the soaking water.** Some of the sugars that cause bloating dissolve into it.
**Cook in fresh water** until soft all the way through. Add salt near the end.
**For moi moi and akara,** soak briefly and rub off the skins, then blend to a smooth paste.

blocks.title: Chemicals on stored beans
blocks.text: Some traders spray stored beans and grains with insecticides to keep weevils away. NAFDAC has warned the public against using pesticides such as dichlorvos to preserve food. Buy from sellers you trust, reject beans with a chemical smell or powdery residue, and wash and soak beans well. Store your own beans in clean, airtight containers in a cool, dry place.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing a yield so you buy the right amount
blocks.context: For example, Amina in Abuja serves a beans and dodo lunch and wants to know how much dry beans she needs for 60 portions of 250 g cooked beans.
steps: She soaks and cooks 1 kg of dry beans and weighs the cooked beans: 2.4 kg. Her yield factor is 2.4.
She needs 60 x 250 g = 15,000 g cooked beans.
Dry beans needed: 15,000 g divided by 2.4 = 6,250 g.
She adds about 5% for sorting losses: 6,250 x 1.05 = about 6,560 g, so she buys 6.5 to 7 kg.
She records the yield factor on her recipe card and re-tests if she changes bean variety.
blocks.result: Amina buys 7 kg of dry beans, enough for 60 full portions with a small margin, instead of guessing.

blocks.text: Proteins that work together

Proteins are built from amino acids. Cereals such as rice and maize are relatively low in one amino acid called lysine. Legumes such as beans and soybeans are richer in lysine but lower in methionine, which cereals supply better. Eating cereals and legumes together, as in rice and beans, moi moi with pap, or akara with bread, gives a better mix of amino acids than either alone. This is useful when animal protein is expensive.

blocks.title: Why rice and beans work together
items: Cereals: rice, maize, acha
Legumes: beans, soy, groundnut
blocks.caption: Each food fills the other's gap, so together they give better quality protein.

blocks.text: Animal proteins such as eggs, fish, chicken and goat meat are complete proteins. Eggs are among the cheapest. Keep them cool and dry, use cracked eggs only in fully cooked dishes, and cook eggs for children, pregnant women and older people until the yolk is firm. Soybeans can be made into soy milk and "awara" (soy cheese), affordable proteins that many Nigerian families already enjoy.

blocks.title: Record your ratios
blocks.text: Keep a page in your recipe book for each grain and bean you buy: brand, water ratio, cooking time and yield factor. That page becomes the reason your food is always consistent.

takeaways: Measure water for rice and acha and record the ratio that works for your brand
Soak beans 6 to 8 hours and discard the soaking water to save fuel and reduce bloating
Use a tested yield factor to buy the right quantity of dry beans or rice
Cereals plus legumes give better quality protein than either alone
Reject beans with a chemical smell and store grains dry and airtight

activity.title: Build your yield page
steps: Cook 1 cup of your usual rice with measured water and note the result.
Soak and cook 500 g of dry beans and weigh the cooked beans.
Calculate the yield factor for the beans.
Use it to calculate the dry beans needed for 40 portions of 200 g.
activity.evidence: Your yield page showing water ratios, yield factor and the 40-portion calculation

lessons.title: Plating and presentation: making food look as good as it tastes
objectives: Plate a Nigerian meal using balance, colour, height and clean edges
Control portions with measured scoops and ladles
Set up an assembly line to plate many meals quickly and identically
Choose garnishes that are edible and match the dish

blocks.text: People eat with their eyes first. Two plates of the same ofada rice and ayamase can earn very different reactions: one heaped untidily with sauce running over the rim, the other neat, colourful and generous. Presentation does not need expensive ingredients. It needs a plan, the right tools and clean habits.

blocks.name: fork-and-knife-with-plate
blocks.alt: A plate with a fork and knife
blocks.caption: A neat, balanced plate signals care before the first bite.

blocks.text: Five principles of a good plate

items: **Balance:** a clear main item, a starch and a vegetable or side. Think of the plate as a clock face: many chefs put the protein at the front (6 o'clock), the starch at the back left and the vegetables at the back right. Keep your layout the same for every plate.

**Colour contrast:** white rice next to green vegetables and red stew looks fresh. Brown food next to brown food looks dull. Add something green or bright, such as sliced cucumber, steamed carrots or fried plantain.
**Height:** a small mound of rice shaped in a bowl or ring mould gives the plate shape. Lean the protein against it.
**Space and clean rims:** leave the rim of the plate empty. Wipe drips with a clean, damp paper towel before serving.
**Sauce control:** spoon stew next to or over part of the protein, not across the whole plate, so the rice stays white and the plate stays clean.

blocks.text: Portion control tools

Portion scoops and ladles are sold by volume, for example a 125 ml or 250 ml ladle. When every plate is filled with the same tools, every customer gets the same amount and your costing stays accurate. Test each tool once: fill it with your rice or stew, weigh the contents, and write the weight on a strip of tape on the handle.

head: Component
Tool
Example tested weight
rows: Bowl or ring mould, packed lightly
Tongs, measured by count or small cup
One small cup of coleslaw or steamed vegetables

blocks.title: Worked example: plating 40 plates for a high table
blocks.context: For example, Yemi in Ibadan is serving 40 plated meals of ofada rice, ayamase, dodo and a boiled egg at an engagement ceremony, with two helpers.
steps: She sets an assembly line on a clean table: plates, then rice station, then sauce and protein station, then sides and garnish, then a wipe-and-check station.
Helper 1 shapes rice with a mould. Helper 2 adds one ladle of ayamase, the protein and the halved egg. Yemi adds five slices of dodo and a sprig of mint or scent leaf, then wipes and checks each rim.
Each station takes about 20 seconds per plate, so a finished plate leaves the line about every 20 seconds once the line is moving.
40 plates x 20 seconds = 800 seconds, about 13 to 14 minutes, plus a minute or two to start the line.
Waiters carry plates out in batches of 8 while the line keeps running, so the first guests are not waiting for the last plate.
blocks.result: All 40 plates are identical and out in about 15 minutes. Yemi takes a photo of the first plate and keeps it beside the line as the model every plate must match.

blocks.title: Before any plate leaves
items: Same layout as model plate
Correct portions by tool
Hot food hot, cold food cold
Rim wiped clean
Garnish edible and fresh
blocks.caption: A quick check at the last station catches mistakes before the guest sees them.

blocks.title: Garnish with purpose
blocks.text: Every garnish should be edible and belong to the dish: scent leaf on pepper soup, sliced spring onion on fried rice, a little fresh pepper on asun. Avoid inedible decorations or flowers you are not sure are safe to eat.
Hygiene while plating

Plating means a lot of hand contact with ready-to-eat food. Wash hands before starting, use tongs and spoons rather than fingers, and wear clean gloves if you must touch food, changing them if you touch money, phones or your face. Keep hot components covered and hot until they are plated, and plate in batches that can be served straight away.

For takeaway packs, the same principles apply. Put sauce in a separate small container or in a compartment so rice stays fluffy, line up the plantain neatly, and close the lid without pressing food against it. A clean sticker with your business name and the dish name finishes the look.

blocks.title: Photograph your best plate
blocks.text: A good photo of your model plate is also your best marketing picture. Shoot in daylight near a window, from slightly above, on a plain background.

takeaways: Use a fixed layout: protein front, starch and vegetables behind
Contrast colours and add height; keep rims clean
Test and label portion tools so every plate is the same
Plate large numbers with an assembly line and a model plate
Garnishes must be edible and match the dish

activity.title: Design and photograph a model plate
steps: Choose one dish you sell and decide its layout on the plate.
Weigh what one scoop or ladle of each component holds and label the tools.
Plate the dish three times and compare the three plates.
Photograph your best plate in daylight and write its portion weights beside the photo.

quiz.q: Ngozi's stew tastes sour and the oil spits when she fries it. What step did she most likely skip?
options: Boiling down the blended tomatoes before frying
Using palm oil instead of vegetable oil
quiz.explain: Fresh tomatoes are mostly water. Boiling the blend down first, then frying until the oil rises, removes water and the raw, sour taste.

quiz.q: A stew base batch weighs 3.6 kg and portions are 120 g. How many portions is that?
quiz.explain: 3,600 g divided by 120 g = 30 portions.

quiz.q: Amina's dry beans have a yield factor of 2.5. How much dry beans does she need for 50 portions of 200 g cooked beans?
quiz.explain: 50 x 200 g = 10,000 g cooked. 10,000 divided by 2.5 = 4,000 g, so 4 kg dry beans (plus a small margin for sorting).

quiz.q: Why is rice and beans together a good protein choice?
options: Beans add lysine that cereals lack, and cereals add methionine
Rice contains more protein than meat
Cooking them together destroys anti-nutrients completely
quiz.explain: Cereals are low in lysine and legumes are low in methionine. Together they give a better amino acid mix.

quiz.q: Which garnish is the best choice for a bowl of goat meat pepper soup?
options: A decorative leaf you have never eaten
quiz.explain: Garnishes must be edible and belong to the dish. Scent leaf is a natural partner for pepper soup.

quiz.q: Yemi's team plates 60 meals at about 20 seconds per plate once the line is moving. About how long will plating take?
quiz.explain: 60 x 20 seconds = 1,200 seconds = 20 minutes, plus a little time to start the line.

modules.title: Nutrition Science for African Families
modules.overview: Good cooking feeds the body as well as pleasing the tongue. This module explains the three macronutrients and how to count energy from a food label, the vitamins and minerals most often lacking in West African diets, how to plan a week of family meals using WHO healthy diet guidance, and how to adapt cooking for family members living with diabetes or high blood pressure, always alongside their health worker's advice.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats: energy, labels and balance
objectives: Explain what carbohydrates, proteins and fats each do in the body
Calculate the energy in a food from its grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat
Estimate a woman's daily protein need from her body weight
Apply WHO limits on free sugars and fats to everyday meals

blocks.text: Every food is made of nutrients. Three of them, **carbohydrates, proteins and fats**, are needed in large amounts and provide energy, so they are called **macronutrients**. Vitamins and minerals are needed in tiny amounts and are called micronutrients; they are the subject of the next lesson. Understanding macronutrients lets you read a food label, judge a plate and plan meals with confidence.

blocks.name: healthy-options
blocks.alt: A woman choosing between food options
blocks.caption: Knowing what each macronutrient does helps you choose and combine foods well.

head: Macronutrient
Main job
Energy per gram
Local sources
rows: Main fuel for brain and muscles
Rice, yam, garri, bread, plantain, maize, fruit
Builds and repairs muscle, blood, skin and the immune system
Beans, fish, eggs, meat, chicken, soy, groundnuts
Concentrated energy; carries vitamins A, D, E and K
Palm oil, groundnut oil, egusi, groundnuts, avocado

blocks.text: Energy in food is measured in kilocalories (kcal), often just called calories. Notice that fat gives more than twice the energy of carbohydrate or protein per gram. That is why oily food is so filling, and why a few extra spoons of oil in every pot add up over a week.
Carbohydrates: quality matters

items: **Starches** in whole grains, yam, beans, plantain and cassava release energy steadily, especially with their fibre intact.
**Fibre** is a carbohydrate the body cannot digest. It keeps bowels regular and helps you feel full. Beans, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, ofada rice and unpolished grains are good sources.

**Free sugars** are sugars added to food and drinks, plus sugar in honey, syrups and fruit juice. WHO recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy, and suggests below 5% for further benefit. Soft drinks and sweetened malt drinks are a major source.

blocks.text: Processing changes carbohydrates. Polished white rice, white bread and garri have lost much of their fibre, so they are digested faster than ofada rice, whole maize or beans. You do not need to give up favourite staples. Serve them in sensible portions alongside beans and vegetables, which slow digestion and keep the family full for longer.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a food label
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Lagos is checking the label on a pack of instant noodles she gives her children. The label says that one 70 g pack contains 45 g carbohydrate, 7 g protein and 14 g fat. (These are illustrative figures; always read your own label.)
steps: Energy from carbohydrate: 45 g x 4 kcal = 180 kcal.
Energy from protein: 7 g x 4 kcal = 28 kcal.
Energy from fat: 14 g x 9 kcal = 126 kcal.
Total energy: 180 + 28 + 126 = 334 kcal.
Share from fat: 126 divided by 334 = 0.38, so about 38% of the energy comes from fat.
blocks.result: Grace sees that the pack is high in fat and low in protein. She adds an egg and some chopped vegetables to raise the protein and fibre and makes it an occasional food rather than daily.

blocks.text: Protein: how much is enough?

For healthy adults, the WHO, FAO and UN University expert report sets a safe level of protein intake of about 0.83 g of good quality protein per kilogram of body weight per day. A woman who weighs 65 kg therefore needs about 65 x 0.83 = 54 g of protein a day. Children, pregnant and breastfeeding women need relatively more for their size, so their health worker's guidance comes first. As a rough picture, 54 g could come from one egg, a portion of beans and a piece of fish over the day.
Fats: type and amount

WHO advises that total fat should be no more than about 30% of daily energy, saturated fat less than 10%, and industrially produced trans fats as low as possible. Trans fats are found in some baked and fried snacks made with partially hydrogenated oils. Palm oil is a valued traditional fat and rich in vitamin A in its red form, but it is high in saturated fat, so measure it rather than pouring freely. Use groundnut, soybean or other vegetable oils for some cooking, and get fats from whole foods like groundnuts and fish.

blocks.title: Energy density of macronutrients
items: Fat: 9 kcal per gram
Protein: 4 kcal per gram
Carbohydrate: 4 kcal per gram
blocks.caption: Small amounts of fat carry a lot of energy, so oil quantity matters most when watching calories.

blocks.title: Measure your oil
blocks.text: Use a measuring spoon or a marked cup for oil when cooking for the family. One tablespoon of oil is roughly 13 to 14 g of fat, about 120 kcal. Cutting two tablespoons from a family pot removes about 240 kcal without changing the dish much.

blocks.title: Balance, not banning
blocks.text: No single food is good or bad on its own. Aim for a plate with a starch, a protein and plenty of vegetables, and keep sugary drinks and very oily snacks occasional.

takeaways: Carbohydrate and protein give 4 kcal per gram, fat gives 9 kcal per gram
Energy from a label = carbs x 4 + protein x 4 + fat x 9
Healthy adults need about 0.83 g of protein per kg body weight per day
WHO: free sugars under 10% of energy, total fat no more than about 30%
Measure cooking oil instead of pouring

activity.title: Label detective
steps: Collect labels from three packaged foods in your home, such as noodles, biscuits and a malt drink.
For each, calculate total energy from carbohydrate, protein and fat.
Calculate the percentage of energy that comes from fat and from sugar where sugar is listed.
Write one change your family could make for each product.
activity.evidence: A photo of the three labels with your calculations written beside each

lessons.title: Iron, vitamin A, iodine and zinc: preventing common deficiencies through food
objectives: Name the micronutrients most often lacking in West African diets and their food sources
Combine foods to improve iron absorption from plant meals
Cook vegetables in ways that keep more vitamins
Explain why supplements should come only with health worker advice

blocks.text: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals the body needs in very small amounts. When they are missing, the effects can be serious: tiredness and poor concentration from anaemia, night blindness and frequent infections from vitamin A deficiency, and poor growth in children. WHO describes iodine, vitamin A and iron deficiencies as among the most important worldwide, zinc deficiency is also common, and women of childbearing age and young children are most at risk.

blocks.name: leafy-green
blocks.caption: Dark leafy vegetables such as ugwu and spinach supply folate, vitamin A and some iron.

head: Nutrient
Why it matters
Good local food sources
rows: Makes haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood; lack causes anaemia
Liver, red meat, fish, chicken, beans, dark leafy greens
Red palm oil, liver, eggs, carrots, orange-fleshed sweet potato, mango, pawpaw, dark leafy greens
Thyroid hormones; brain development of babies in the womb
Meat, fish, crayfish, beans, groundnuts, whole grains
Making new cells; important before and in early pregnancy
Dark leafy greens, beans, groundnuts, oranges

blocks.text: Getting more iron out of your food

Iron in meat, fish and chicken (called **haem iron**) is absorbed well. Iron in beans, grains and vegetables (**non-haem iron**) is absorbed less well, but what you eat with it makes a big difference. Vitamin C in the same meal helps the body absorb non-haem iron. Tea and coffee contain compounds that reduce iron absorption when drunk with meals. Even a small piece of fish or meat in a bean dish improves absorption of the iron from the beans.

blocks.title: What helps and what hinders iron absorption
items: Helps iron absorption
Reduces iron absorption
left: Orange, pawpaw or guava with meals
Tomatoes and peppers in the dish
A little fish or meat with beans
right: Large milk drinks at iron-rich meals
blocks.caption: The same plate of beans gives the body more iron when paired with vitamin C and no tea.

blocks.title: Worked example: improving a teenage daughter's meals
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Jos notices her 15-year-old daughter is often tired. The clinic has checked her and advised more iron-rich food. Her usual day is tea and bread in the morning, rice and stew at school, and garri with sugar in the evening.
steps: Breakfast: Esther swaps tea for pap made with a spoon of ground crayfish or groundnut, plus a slice of pawpaw. Tea moves to mid-morning, at least an hour away from meals.
School lunch: she packs rice with beans instead of rice alone, and adds sliced tomato and cucumber.
Evening: three nights a week she cooks efo riro or ugwu soup with fish or a small piece of liver, served with an orange.
Weekly check: she plans liver or red meat at least once and beans at least three times, and writes it on the family meal plan.
blocks.result: Without buying expensive foods, the daughter now gets iron at every meal, with vitamin C alongside and tea away from meals. Esther keeps follow-up appointments as the clinic advised.

blocks.text: Cooking to keep vitamins

items: **Wash vegetables before cutting, not after.** Washing cut leaves rinses away water-soluble vitamins.
**Cook leafy vegetables briefly** and add them near the end of cooking.
**Use little water and cover the pot.** Vitamins leak into cooking water; use that water in the soup instead of pouring it away.
**Avoid adding potash (kaun) or baking soda** to keep vegetables green; alkalis destroy some vitamins, including vitamin C.
**Pair vitamin A foods with a little fat.** Vitamin A is fat-soluble, so a little oil in vegetable soup helps the body absorb it.
**Use iodised salt, stored covered** away from heat and sunlight, and add it towards the end of cooking.

blocks.text: Red palm oil deserves special mention. It is one of the richest local sources of beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A. Very long, high heating destroys much of it, so soups cooked gently with red palm oil keep more of this value than oil that has been heated until pale. A little goes a long way.

blocks.title: Supplements need a health worker
blocks.text: Do not give iron, vitamin A or other supplements to children or adults on your own guesswork. Too much iron is poisonous to young children, and too much vitamin A is harmful, especially in pregnancy. In Nigeria, routine supplements such as iron and folic acid in pregnancy and vitamin A for young children are given through antenatal clinics and health facilities. Follow their advice and keep all supplements locked away from children.

blocks.title: Fermenting and soaking help
blocks.text: Soaking, sprouting and fermenting grains and legumes, as in ogi or iru, reduce phytates, natural compounds that bind iron and zinc. Traditional methods have real nutritional value.

If someone in your family shows signs such as constant tiredness, pale inner eyelids, breathlessness, or poor sight in dim light, take them to a health facility. Food helps prevent deficiencies, but diagnosis and treatment belong to health workers.

takeaways: Iron, vitamin A, iodine and zinc deficiencies are common, especially for women and young children
Eat vitamin C foods with plant iron and drink tea between meals, not with them
Wash before cutting, cook greens briefly, and avoid potash in vegetables
Use iodised salt and a little fat with vitamin A foods
Supplements only on health worker advice; keep them away from children

lessons.title: Planning a week of balanced family meals on a budget
objectives: Apply WHO healthy diet guidance on fruit, vegetables, salt and sugar to a family menu
Build a 7-day meal plan and a shopping list from it
Plan meals for young children in line with WHO feeding guidance
Use batch cooking to save time, fuel and money

blocks.text: Families who plan meals usually eat better and spend less. Without a plan, the evening question "what are we eating?" leads to last-minute buying, the same three dishes repeated, and more noodles and soft drinks than anyone intended. A simple weekly plan fixes this in about 30 minutes a week.

blocks.name: eating-together
blocks.alt: A family eating together at a table
blocks.caption: A weekly plan turns healthy eating into a family routine rather than a daily struggle.

blocks.text: The WHO healthy diet targets

items: **Fruit and vegetables:** at least 400 g a day for adults, about five portions. Starchy roots such as yam, cassava and potato do not count towards this.
**Salt:** less than 5 g a day for adults, which is just under one level teaspoon, and use iodised salt. Remember that seasoning cubes and salty snacks add salt too.
**Free sugars:** less than 10% of energy. In practice: water instead of soft drinks, and sweets and sugary drinks as treats.
**Fats:** prefer unsaturated oils, limit fried snacks and avoid industrially produced trans fats.
**Variety:** staples, legumes, vegetables, fruit and animal foods across the week.

blocks.text: Feeding babies and young children

WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then nutritious complementary foods from 6 months while breastfeeding continues up to 2 years or beyond. A baby's first foods should be soft and thick enough to stay on a spoon, such as pap enriched with groundnut paste or crayfish powder, mashed beans, or mashed yam with a little fish and oil. Do not add salt or sugar to a baby's food. Wash hands, bowls and spoons carefully, and give freshly prepared food.
Building the plan

items: **List your family's favourite dishes** and the ingredients in season and cheap now.
**Fill a 7-day grid** for breakfast, lunch and dinner. Each day should include a legume or animal protein, at least two vegetable servings and one fruit.
**Plan cook-once, eat-twice meals:** a big pot of soup on Sunday serves Sunday and Tuesday; stew base made on Monday serves rice on Monday and beans on Wednesday.
**Write a shopping list by market section** with quantities, and check what you already have.
**Prepare ahead:** pick and wash vegetables, soak beans the night before, portion and freeze proteins.

head: Day
Breakfast
Lunch
Dinner
rows: Pap with akara and a slice of pawpaw
Rice and beans with stew, sliced cucumber
Efo riro with fish and eba, an orange
Boiled yam with egg sauce full of tomato and onion
Moi moi with pap and a banana
Bread, boiled egg and an orange
Beans with Monday's stew base and dodo
Okra soup with fish and fufu, watermelon

blocks.text: Notice how the sample days reuse work: Monday's stew base appears again on Wednesday, and Sunday's soup returns on Tuesday. Each day has a legume or animal protein, vegetables in at least two meals, and fruit. Once your grid is full, put an approximate price beside each ingredient on the shopping list. If the total is above your budget, swap a costly protein for beans or eggs on one or two days rather than dropping vegetables.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much fruit and vegetables to buy
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Benin City plans meals for herself, her husband and three children aged 9, 12 and 15. She wants to reach the WHO target of at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day.
steps: She uses 400 g a day per person as a simple target for all five, knowing the youngest may eat a little less.
Daily need: 5 x 400 g = 2,000 g, that is 2 kg a day.
Weekly need: 2 kg x 7 = 14 kg of fruit and vegetables.
She splits it: about 6 kg of leafy and other vegetables for soups and sides (ugwu, efo, okra, garden egg, carrots, cabbage), and about 8 kg of fruit (oranges, bananas, pawpaw, watermelon in season).
She buys twice a week, 7 kg each trip, so produce stays fresh, and chooses whatever fruit is in season and cheapest.
blocks.result: Blessing turns a health guideline into a concrete shopping quantity. Her market list now has 7 kg of produce on Saturdays and Wednesdays.

blocks.title: The weekly meal planning cycle
items: Plan 7-day grid
Write shopping list
Shop and prep ahead
Cook and serve
Review leftovers and likes
blocks.caption: Each week's review makes the next plan cheaper and more popular with the family.

blocks.title: Leftovers are planned food
blocks.text: Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours and eat them within a day or two. Reheat until steaming hot throughout. Plan one "leftover night" each week so nothing is wasted.

blocks.title: Nigerian guidance
blocks.text: The Federal Ministry of Health has published food-based dietary guidelines for Nigeria. Health workers at your primary health care centre can advise on family and child feeding in line with national guidance.

takeaways: Aim for at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables per adult per day
Less than 5 g salt a day, including salt from seasoning cubes
Exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months, then nutritious complementary foods with no added salt or sugar
A 7-day grid plus a shopping list saves money and repeats fewer dishes
Cook once, eat twice: batch cook and plan leftovers
