objectives: Cut salt in family cooking while keeping dishes tasty
Use the healthy plate method to portion meals for someone with diabetes
Adapt common Nigerian dishes for these conditions
Work alongside, never instead of, the advice of a doctor, nurse or dietitian

blocks.text: Diabetes and high blood pressure (hypertension) are common in Nigerian families. Food is a central part of managing both. As the cook, you have real influence: the amount of salt, oil and sugar in the family pot, the size of the swallow portion, and how many vegetables reach the plate. This lesson shows practical changes. It does not replace medical care. Anyone with these conditions should follow their health worker's plan and take medicines exactly as prescribed.

blocks.name: healthy-lifestyle
blocks.alt: A person living a healthy lifestyle
blocks.caption: Small, steady changes in the family kitchen support the care plan from the clinic.

blocks.text: High blood pressure: the salt problem

Eating too much salt (sodium) raises blood pressure. WHO advises adults to eat less than 5 g of salt a day, just under one level teaspoon, and lowering salt is one of the most effective diet changes for people with hypertension. In many Nigerian kitchens, salt comes from three places: salt added in the pot, seasoning cubes, and salty foods such as some processed meats, snacks and salted fish. Eating more vegetables and fruit, which contain potassium, also helps, unless a health worker has advised limiting potassium, for example because of kidney disease.

blocks.title: Worked example: lowering the salt in a pot of soup
blocks.context: For example, Joy in Calabar cooks a pot of edikang ikong that serves 10 portions over two days. Her father has high blood pressure. She usually adds 3 level teaspoons of salt plus 4 seasoning cubes.
steps: A level teaspoon of salt weighs roughly 5 g, so 3 teaspoons is about 15 g of added salt.
Per portion from added salt alone: 15 g divided by 10 = about 1.5 g, before counting the cubes, stockfish, periwinkle and other salty ingredients.
She cuts the salt to 1.5 teaspoons (about 7.5 g) and the cubes from 4 to 1. Added salt per portion falls to about 0.75 g plus a little from one cube.
She builds flavour instead with homemade stock, crayfish, a little iru, fresh pepper and plenty of vegetables.
She soaks dried fish and stockfish well to wash out some of the salt, and keeps the salt shaker off the table.
blocks.result: The soup still tastes rich, the whole family eats less salt, and her father's portion fits more easily into his salt limit. Tastes adjust over a few weeks, so she cuts down gradually.

blocks.text: Diabetes: steady carbohydrates and the healthy plate

In diabetes, the body cannot control blood sugar properly. Carbohydrate foods raise blood sugar the most, so the amount and type matter. The **healthy plate method**, used by many diabetes educators, is simple: fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables, a quarter with protein, and a quarter with the starchy food. For many Nigerian families the big change is the swallow: the mound of eba, pounded yam or fufu is often much larger than a quarter of the plate.

blocks.title: The healthy plate for diabetes
items: Half: non-starchy vegetables
Quarter: fish, beans, egg, chicken
Quarter: swallow, rice or yam
Water instead of sweet drinks
Regular meal times
blocks.caption: Changing the proportions on the plate is often easier than changing the dishes.

items: **Portion the swallow** with a scoop or a small bowl so it is the same size every meal. Increase the soup and vegetables instead.
**Choose more fibre:** beans, unpolished or ofada rice, whole maize, vegetables and whole fruit rather than juice.
**Cut sugary drinks** entirely: soft drinks, sweetened malt drinks and juices raise blood sugar quickly. Offer water or unsweetened zobo.
**Eat regularly** and do not skip meals, especially for people on medicines that lower blood sugar. Ask the health worker about meal timing.
**Mind the oil:** fried foods add a lot of energy; boil, grill or steam more often.

head: Usual choice
Adapted choice
rows: Large mound of pounded yam with soup
Smaller measured swallow, extra vegetable soup and fish
Boiled or roasted plantain with an omelette full of vegetables
Moi moi or boiled egg with vegetables, unsweetened tea

blocks.text: Keep a simple record for a month: what the person ate on days their readings were good or poor, if they check blood sugar or blood pressure at home as their health worker advised. Bring the record to the clinic. It helps the nurse, doctor or dietitian give advice that fits your family's real meals.

blocks.title: Never change medicines through food
blocks.text: Do not stop or change any prescribed medicine because the diet has improved, and do not use herbal mixtures sold as cures for diabetes or hypertension. If someone on diabetes medicine feels shaky, sweaty or confused, they may have low blood sugar and need quick help as their health worker has advised. Keep their clinic appointments.

blocks.title: Cook one pot, serve two ways
blocks.text: You do not need separate meals. Cook the family pot with less salt and oil, then let others add a little more at the table if they wish, while the person with the condition takes the adapted portion.

takeaways: WHO advises less than 5 g of salt a day; seasoning cubes count
Cut salt gradually and build flavour with stock, crayfish, iru and herbs
Healthy plate: half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter starch
Replace sugary drinks with water and measure the swallow
Food supports medical care; never change medicines without the health worker

activity.title: Adapt one family dish
steps: Choose a dish your family eats every week.
Write down how much salt, cubes and oil you usually add.
Cook it with half the salt and cubes, adding herbs or crayfish for flavour.
Serve one portion using the healthy plate method and photograph it.
Ask the family to rate the taste and note their comments.
activity.evidence: Before and after ingredient amounts, the plate photo and the family's comments

quiz.q: A snack label shows 20 g carbohydrate, 3 g protein and 10 g fat per pack. How many kcal is that?
Roughly how much protein does a healthy 70 kg adult need each day, using about 0.83 g per kg?
quiz.explain: 70 x 0.83 = 58.1 g, so about 58 g a day.

quiz.q: Kemi serves beans for lunch and wants her body to absorb more of the iron. What is the best drink with the meal?
options: Fresh orange juice or an orange
quiz.explain: Vitamin C helps absorb plant iron. Tea, coffee and large milk drinks taken with the meal reduce absorption.

quiz.q: Which habit keeps more vitamins in vegetable soup?
options: Cutting vegetables, then washing them well
Adding potash to keep leaves green
Boiling leaves for a long time
Washing before cutting and adding leaves near the end
quiz.explain: Washing after cutting rinses vitamins away, potash destroys some vitamins and long boiling damages them.

quiz.q: A family of 4 adults wants to meet the WHO target for fruit and vegetables. How much should they buy per week?
quiz.explain: 4 x 400 g = 1.6 kg a day. 1.6 kg x 7 = 11.2 kg a week.

quiz.q: Uncle Femi has diabetes. Which plate follows the healthy plate method?
options: Three quarters eba, a quarter soup
Half vegetables, a quarter fish, a quarter eba
Rice only, with a soft drink
quiz.explain: Half non-starchy vegetables, a quarter protein and a quarter starch is the healthy plate method.

quiz.q: Joy's father's blood pressure readings improved after the family cut salt. What should he do about his medicine?
options: Stop it, because the diet is working
Keep taking it as prescribed and discuss it at his next clinic visit
Replace it with a herbal mixture
quiz.explain: Only the health worker should change medicines. Diet supports treatment; it does not replace it.

modules.title: Food Preservation and Packaged Products
modules.overview: Preserving food lets you buy produce when it is cheap, cut waste and create products that sell between events. This module covers drying fruit, vegetables and spices with yield calculations, fermenting ogi and vegetables and making vinegar pickles safely, and formulating jarred pepper sauce and dry spice blends such as yaji and pepper soup spice that taste the same in every pack.

lessons.title: Drying tomatoes, ginger, mango and leafy vegetables
objectives: Explain why removing water stops spoilage
Prepare, pre-treat and dry tomatoes, ginger, mango and leafy vegetables
Calculate dried yield from the water content of fresh produce
Test dryness and store dried food so it stays safe

blocks.text: Bacteria, moulds and yeasts need water to grow. When you remove enough water from food, they cannot multiply, and the food keeps for months instead of days. Drying is one of the oldest preservation methods in Africa: think of dried okra, crayfish, stockfish and dried pepper. In this lesson you will use the same principle on products that fetch good prices in towns: dried tomato, dried ginger, mango slices and dried leafy vegetables.

blocks.name: tomato
blocks.caption: Fresh tomatoes are about 94% water; drying removes most of it so the product keeps for months.

blocks.text: Open sun, solar dryer or oven?

head: Method
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Open sun on mats or roofs
Dust, insects, birds, rain; slow; uneven
Solar cabinet dryer (box with clear cover and mesh trays)
Faster and cleaner, protected from insects and rain
Needs building or buying; still depends on weather
Electric or oven drying at low heat
Controlled, works at night and in rainy season
Electricity or gas cost; small capacity

blocks.text: For a product you sell, a covered solar dryer with food-grade mesh trays is the minimum standard. Open-air drying on the ground or by the roadside exposes food to dust, animal droppings and vehicle fumes. Whatever method you use, air must move over the food: heat removes water from the surface, and moving air carries it away.
Preparing each product

items: **Tomatoes:** choose firm, ripe, unbruised fruit. Wash, cut into slices about 6 to 8 mm thick, or halves for small tomatoes. Thin, even slices dry evenly.
**Ginger:** wash and scrub, then slice thinly. Dried slices can be ground into ginger powder for spice blends and drinks.
**Mango:** peel and slice 6 to 8 mm thick. Dipping slices briefly in lemon juice diluted with water reduces browning.

**Leafy vegetables (ugwu, spinach, bitter leaf):** wash whole leaves, then **blanch** them: dip in boiling water for about 1 to 2 minutes and cool quickly in clean cold water. Blanching keeps colour and slows enzyme damage during drying.
**Spread in a single layer** with space between pieces, and turn them once or twice.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much dried tomato from 10 kg?
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Kaduna buys tomatoes cheaply at the height of the season and wants to sell dried tomato in 100 g packs. Fresh tomatoes are roughly 94% water.
steps: Dry matter in 10 kg fresh tomatoes: 6% of 10 kg = 0.6 kg. That is the part that does not evaporate.
She dries to about 10% moisture, so dry matter will be 90% of the final weight.
Final weight = 0.6 kg divided by 0.90 = about 0.67 kg, that is 670 g.
So 10 kg of fresh tomatoes gives about six 100 g packs, with a little left for testing.
Costs (approximate): tomatoes N10,000, packs and labels N1,500, so about N11,500 for six packs, or about N1,900 per pack before her time and profit.
blocks.result: Zainab now knows that dried tomato is about one fifteenth of its fresh weight. She prices her packs from this figure instead of assuming she will get 1 or 2 kg.

blocks.title: From fresh produce to dried packs
items: Sort, wash, slice evenly
Pre-treat: blanch or dip
Dry in single layers
Test dryness and condition
Pack airtight, label, date
blocks.caption: Every stage either protects quality or protects safety; skipping one shows up weeks later as mould.

blocks.text: Is it dry enough?

items: **Vegetables and ginger** should be brittle or crisp and snap when bent.
**Fruit such as mango** should be leathery and pliable, with no moisture when you tear a piece and squeeze it.
**Conditioning:** pack cooled, dried fruit loosely in a closed jar for about a week and shake it daily. If drops of water form inside the lid, it is not dry enough: return it to the dryer.
**Always cool before packing.** Warm food packed in a bag sweats and goes mouldy.

blocks.title: Mould means discard
blocks.text: Throw away any batch with visible mould, a musty smell or insect damage. Do not pick off the mouldy pieces and sell the rest: some moulds produce toxins that you cannot see or remove. Keep drying trays, knives and packing surfaces clean, and wash hands before handling dried food, because it will not be cooked again before some customers eat it.

Store dried products in airtight, food-grade bags or jars in a cool, dark, dry place. Light fades colour and heat speeds loss of flavour. Write the product name and drying date on each pack, and keep a small sample of each batch so you can check it if a customer complains.

blocks.title: Dry in the dry season
blocks.text: Drying is fastest and safest in the dry season and harmattan, when humidity is low. In the rainy season, plan for a covered or oven method, or buy less fresh produce.

takeaways: Removing water stops microbes growing
Use a covered solar dryer with clean mesh trays, not the open ground
Blanch leafy vegetables; dip fruit in diluted lemon juice to limit browning
Dried weight = dry matter divided by (1 minus final moisture)
Test dryness, condition fruit, cool before packing and discard mouldy batches

activity.title: Dry and weigh one product
steps: Weigh 1 to 2 kg of tomatoes, ginger, mango or leafy vegetables before preparing them.
Prepare and dry them, recording the method, dates and weather.
Test dryness, cool and weigh the dried product.
Calculate your actual yield as a percentage of fresh weight and compare with the expected figure.
activity.evidence: Before and after weights, your yield calculation and a photo of the packed product with its label

lessons.title: Fermenting ogi and vegetables, and making vinegar pickles safely
objectives: Explain how lactic acid fermentation preserves food
Make ogi (akamu) from maize with clean, repeatable steps
Calculate salt for a fermented vegetable brine
Make quick vinegar pickles and know when a ferment must be discarded

blocks.text: Fermentation uses friendly microbes to change food. In **lactic acid fermentation**, bacteria naturally present on grains and vegetables turn sugars into lactic acid. The acid gives the sour taste of ogi, and it makes the food too acidic for many harmful bacteria to grow. West Africa has a rich fermentation tradition: ogi, iru and dawadawa, ugba, fufu, garri and kunu all depend on it.

blocks.name: jar
blocks.caption: Clean jars, the right salt or acid level and good hygiene make fermentation safe and repeatable.

blocks.text: Ogi (akamu) step by step

items: **Sort and wash** dry maize (or millet or sorghum for other types of ogi). Remove stones and mouldy grains.
**Steep** the grain in clean water in a covered container for 1 to 3 days, changing the water daily, until the grains are soft enough to crush with your fingers.
**Wet mill** the softened grain at a clean mill, or blend it in small batches with water.
**Sieve** through a fine cloth or mesh with plenty of clean water. The fibre (husk) stays behind; the starchy liquid passes through.
**Settle and sour:** leave the liquid covered for 1 to 3 days. The starch settles and sours. Pour off the water on top.
**Store** the wet ogi cake covered with a thin layer of clean water, changing it daily, or press it in a cloth bag. Keep it cool and use within a few days.

blocks.title: A typical ogi production week
items: Day 1: sort, wash, steep
Day 2 to 3: change water
Day 3: mill and sieve
Day 4 to 5: settle and sour
Day 5: drain, pack, sell
blocks.caption: Planning the steps across the week lets you sell fresh ogi on fixed days.

blocks.text: Fresh ogi has a clean, pleasantly sour smell. Ogi that smells putrid, looks pink, grey or black, or has fuzzy mould must be thrown away. Sieving fibre removes some nutrients, so many families enrich pap with groundnut paste, crayfish powder or soy flour when they cook it, especially for children.
Salt-brined vegetables

Cabbage, carrots, cucumbers and garden eggs can be fermented in salt. Salt draws out juice, slows unwanted microbes and lets lactic acid bacteria take over. Too little salt and the vegetables go soft and smell bad; too much and fermentation stalls. Many tested recipes use about 2% to 2.5% salt by weight. Weigh the salt; spoons vary too much.

blocks.title: Worked example: salting a cabbage and carrot ferment
blocks.context: For example, Ruth in Jos wants to make a spicy fermented slaw to sell to two restaurants that serve grills.
steps: She shreds 1,800 g of cabbage and 200 g of carrots: 2,000 g of vegetables in total.
At 2% salt: 2,000 g x 0.02 = 40 g of fine salt with no anti-caking additives.
She mixes and massages the salt in until juice comes out, adds sliced scotch bonnet and ginger, and packs it tightly into a clean jar so the juice covers the vegetables.
She weighs the vegetables down under the brine with a smaller clean jar filled with water, covers loosely and keeps it at room temperature out of the sun.
She tastes it from day 3. When it is pleasantly sour, about day 5 to 7 in warm weather, she moves it to the fridge.
blocks.result: Ruth has a repeatable recipe: 2% salt by weight, vegetables kept under the brine, refrigerated once sour. She records the date and taste each time.

blocks.text: Quick vinegar pickles

Vinegar pickles do not rely on fermentation. The acid from the vinegar preserves the vegetables directly. Use vinegar labelled 5% acidity, and follow a tested recipe for the vinegar to water ratio; do not dilute it more than the recipe says, because the acid level is what keeps the pickle safe. For a simple refrigerator pickle, pour hot brine of equal parts 5% vinegar and water, with salt and a little sugar, over sliced cucumber, onion or carrot in a clean jar, cool, and keep it in the fridge.

blocks.title: When to throw a ferment away
blocks.text: A thin white film on the surface of a brine is often a harmless yeast and can be skimmed, but fuzzy mould of any colour, a slimy texture, a rotten smell or pink, black or grey patches mean the batch must be discarded. Never taste a ferment that smells bad. Use only clean water, clean jars and clean hands. Low-acid foods such as plain vegetables in oil are not made safe by this method.

blocks.title: Check acidity with pH strips
blocks.text: Cheap pH test strips let you check that a ferment or pickle has become acidic. Food safety guidance treats a pH of 4.6 or below as the line below which botulism bacteria cannot grow; well-made pickles usually measure lower.

takeaways: Lactic acid bacteria turn sugars into acid, which preserves the food
Ogi: steep, change water daily, mill, sieve, settle and sour, then keep cool
Brined vegetables: about 2% to 2.5% salt by weight, kept under the brine
Vinegar pickles need 5% acidity vinegar and a tested ratio
Discard ferments with fuzzy mould, slime, coloured patches or a rotten smell

activity.title: Make one ferment and one pickle
steps: Weigh 1 kg of shredded vegetables and calculate 2% salt.
Pack the ferment under its brine and record the date and room conditions.
Make a small jar of refrigerator vinegar pickle using 5% vinegar.
Check and taste the ferment daily from day 3, and test both with pH strips if you have them.
activity.evidence: Your salt calculation, a daily log of the ferment, and photos of both jars

lessons.title: Formulating jarred pepper sauce, yaji and pepper soup spice for sale
objectives: Write a spice blend formula in percentages and scale it to any batch size
Grind, mix and pack dry spice blends hygienically
Prepare and hot-fill a cooked pepper sauce into sterilised jars
Identify the allergens and storage instructions your labels must show

blocks.text: Condiments are a smart product for a food business: they use cheap raw materials, they are light to deliver, and customers buy them again and again. Suya spice (yaji), pepper soup spice, and jarred pepper sauces such as shito-style or ata din din are popular in Nigerian cities and with Nigerians abroad. The secret to a condiment business is **consistency**: the hundredth jar must taste exactly like the first.

blocks.name: hot-pepper
blocks.caption: Peppers and spices are the base of condiments that customers rebuy every week.

blocks.text: Write formulas in percentages

Write every recipe as a percentage of the total weight. Then any batch, from 500 g to 20 kg, is just multiplication. Weigh every ingredient on a digital scale. Keep a master formula sheet and a batch record for each production day.

blocks.title: Worked example: scaling a yaji formula to 5 kg
blocks.context: For example, Hadiza in Zaria has perfected her suya spice. Her formula is: kuli kuli (roasted groundnut cake) powder 55%, ground dried chilli 20%, ginger powder 10%, garlic powder 5%, onion powder 5%, salt 5%.
steps: Check the percentages add up: 55 + 20 + 10 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 100%.
For a 5,000 g batch: kuli kuli 5,000 x 0.55 = 2,750 g; chilli 5,000 x 0.20 = 1,000 g; ginger 500 g; garlic 250 g; onion 250 g; salt 250 g.
At 100 g per pack she gets 50 packs. Ingredient cost (approximate) is N27,500, and packs and labels about N7,500. Total N35,000.
Cost per pack: N35,000 divided by 50 = N700 before her time, gas, transport and profit.
blocks.result: Hadiza can make any quantity with identical taste and knows her cost per pack. Because the main ingredient is groundnut, her label must state the groundnut allergen clearly.

head: Blend
Typical ingredients (vary by region and family)
Storage note
rows: Kuli kuli powder, dried chilli, ginger, garlic, onion, salt, sometimes seasoning
Contains groundnut; groundnut fat can go rancid, so pack airtight and date it
Calabash nutmeg (ehuru), grains of selim (uda), uziza seed, alligator pepper, dried chilli
Toast whole spices lightly, cool, then grind
Tatashe, scotch bonnet, onion, oil, sometimes crayfish or locust beans
Cooked sauce; needs sterilised jars and fridge after opening

blocks.text: Hygiene for dry blends

items: **Use only clean, dry, sound raw materials.** Reject mouldy chilli, damp spices and groundnuts that look shrivelled, discoloured or mouldy.
**Dry everything fully before grinding.** Any moisture causes caking and mould in the pack.
**Grind with clean, dry equipment.** If you use a public mill, ask for a clean run or clean it yourself, because shared mills carry other people's ingredients and allergens.
**Mix thoroughly** in a large clean bowl, then pack straight into airtight food-grade pouches or jars.
**Wear a hair cover and clean clothes,** and a dust mask when grinding chilli.

blocks.text: Jarred pepper sauce: cook, fill hot, chill after opening

blocks.title: Hot-filling a pepper sauce
items: Wash and sterilise jars
Cook sauce thoroughly
Fill hot, 1 cm headspace
Cap at once, cool
Label: refrigerate after opening
blocks.caption: Each step reduces the chance of microbes surviving or getting into the jar.

blocks.text: To sterilise jars, wash them in hot soapy water, rinse, then submerge in boiling water for 10 minutes and keep them hot until filling. Boil new lids briefly or follow the maker's instructions. Fill the sauce while it is still very hot, leaving about 1 cm of space at the top, wipe the rim with a clean cloth, and close at once.

blocks.title: Oil-based sauces need extra care
blocks.text: Sauces where garlic, onion, pepper or herbs sit under oil can, if not cooked and acidified properly, allow Clostridium botulinum to grow without air. Botulism is rare but can be fatal. Cook the sauce thoroughly, consider adding vinegar or lemon juice as tested recipes do, keep opened jars in the fridge, and do not claim months of shelf life at room temperature unless a food laboratory has tested your product. NAFDAC can advise on the testing needed before registration.

blocks.title: Labels for condiments
blocks.text: Your label should give the product name, ingredients in descending order of weight, allergens such as groundnut, crayfish or shrimp highlighted, net weight, batch number, production and best before dates, storage instructions, and your name and address. Module 5 covers registration.

Run a simple shelf-life check before selling widely: keep three jars or packs from a batch, store them as a customer would, and open one at intervals. Record the smell, colour, taste and any mould. Set your best before date well inside the time your samples stayed good, and repeat the check whenever you change the recipe or packaging.

takeaways: Write every formula in percentages and weigh every ingredient
Scale by multiplying the batch weight by each percentage, then check the total
Dry blends must be fully dry, ground on clean equipment and packed airtight
Hot-fill cooked sauces into sterilised jars and label them to refrigerate after opening
Declare allergens such as groundnut and crayfish on the label

activity.title: Formulate and scale your own blend
steps: Write your spice blend or sauce as percentages adding to 100%.
Scale it to a 1 kg test batch and weigh every ingredient.
Make, pack and label five test packs or jars.
Calculate the cost per pack and get feedback from three people.
activity.evidence: Your formula sheet, batch record, cost per pack and a photo of the labelled packs

quiz.q: Fresh ginger is about 80% water. Zara dries 5 kg to about 10% moisture. About how much dried ginger will she get?
quiz.explain: Dry matter = 20% of 5 kg = 1 kg. Final weight = 1 divided by 0.90 = about 1.1 kg.

quiz.q: Why should leafy vegetables be blanched before drying?
options: To keep colour and slow enzyme damage
To make them dry faster in the rain
To remove all bacteria for life
quiz.explain: Brief blanching in boiling water, then quick cooling, keeps colour and slows enzyme changes during drying.

quiz.q: Ruth has 3 kg of shredded cabbage for a 2% salt ferment. How much salt does she need?
quiz.explain: 3,000 g x 0.02 = 60 g of salt.

quiz.q: Bisi opens her ogi container and sees pink patches and fuzzy growth. What should she do?
options: Skim the top and sell the rest
Cook it longer to kill the mould
quiz.explain: Fuzzy mould and coloured patches mean the batch is spoiled. It must be thrown away.

quiz.q: A pepper soup spice formula is 40% calabash nutmeg, 30% grains of selim, 20% uziza seed and 10% chilli. How much uziza seed is needed for a 2.5 kg batch?
Which instruction belongs on a jar of homemade ata din din?
options: Keeps for two years at room temperature
quiz.explain: Cooked oil-based sauces should be kept in the fridge once opened. Long room-temperature claims need laboratory testing.

modules.title: Running a Home Catering and Food Products Business
modules.overview: This module turns your cooking skills into a business that runs smoothly and legally. You will plan staff, equipment and service style for an event, cost recipes properly using yield and food cost percentage and analyse which menu items earn you the most, and build the registration, hygiene and record-keeping pack that clients, inspectors and NAFDAC expect.

lessons.title: Event operations: service style, staffing, equipment and gas safety
objectives: Choose between buffet, plated, family-style and packed service for an event
Calculate staff and buffet lines for a given number of guests
Build an equipment list and an event-day run sheet
Set up and use LPG cylinders and burners safely at an event venue

blocks.text: Cooking well is only half of event catering. The other half is **operations**: getting the right food, people and equipment to the right place, serving every guest within a reasonable time, and leaving the venue clean. Many caterers lose clients not because the food was poor, but because the queue was long, food ran out on one side of the hall, or servers did not know what to do.

blocks.name: special-event
blocks.caption: Smooth service at an event depends on planning staff, lines and equipment as carefully as the menu.

blocks.text: Choosing a service style

blocks.title: Buffet or plated service?
items: Buffet
Plated
blocks.caption: Many Nigerian events mix both: plated service for the high table and a buffet or packs for other guests.

blocks.text: **Family style** places shared dishes on each table and suits small, intimate events. **Packed service** (food in takeaway packs or food flasks) is common at large Nigerian parties because it is fast to distribute, but it needs very careful timing so hot food is not packed hours ahead and left warm.
Staffing rules of thumb

Caterers use rough guides and then adjust for the venue and the client. A common rule of thumb is about one server for every 10 to 15 guests for plated service, and one server for every 25 to 30 guests at a staffed buffet, plus kitchen staff and at least one supervisor who does not serve. Many caterers plan one buffet line, served from both sides if possible, for every 75 to 100 guests so that queues stay short.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a 300-guest wedding buffet
blocks.context: For example, Patience in Uyo is catering a wedding reception for 300 guests: plated service for 20 at the high table and a staffed buffet for 280.
steps: Buffet lines: 280 guests divided by about 90 per line = 3.1, so she sets up 3 double-sided lines.
Buffet servers: 280 divided by 28 = 10 servers, so 3 per line plus one to refill.
High table: 20 guests at 1 server per 10 = 2 servers.
Kitchen and support: 2 people plating and refilling chafing dishes, 2 runners for drinks and clearing, 1 supervisor. Total team: 10 + 2 + 5 = 17.
Chafing dishes: 5 hot items per line x 3 lines = 15 chafing dishes, plus 2 spares in case a fuel gel runs out or a dish is damaged.
blocks.result: Patience quotes for 17 staff and 17 chafing dishes instead of guessing, briefs each person on their station, and her team serves 280 buffet guests in good time.

blocks.text: Equipment list and run sheet

items: **Cooking:** burners, pots with lids, gas cylinders, regulators and hoses, cooking spoons, chopping boards in separate colours for raw and cooked food.
**Holding and service:** chafing dishes with fuel, insulated food flasks or coolers, serving spoons and tongs (one per dish), food probe thermometer.
**Hygiene:** handwashing station with soap and clean water, paper towels, gloves, hair covers, aprons, refuse bags, cleaning cloths and sanitiser.
**Paperwork:** the menu, guest count, run sheet, staff list with phone numbers, and the client contact on the day.

blocks.text: Keeping food safe from kitchen to guest

Timing is the main food safety tool at events. Cook as close to service as you can, transport hot food in insulated flasks or covered pots that are full and tightly closed, and check the temperature on arrival with your probe thermometer. Hot food should stay above 60 C during service. Light chafing dish fuel 15 to 20 minutes before the lines open so the water underneath is already hot, and top up dishes with fresh hot food rather than mixing new food into old.

Agree with the client in advance what happens to leftovers. Food that has stood on a buffet for hours should not be packed for guests to take home. Throw away anything that has been out of temperature control for more than 2 hours.

A **run sheet** is a timed list of what happens and who does it: when the van leaves, when the team arrives, when lines open, when the cake is cut, when service closes and when the team must leave the hall. Share it on your team WhatsApp group the day before and print one copy for the supervisor.

blocks.title: LPG gas at venues
blocks.text: Keep gas cylinders upright, outdoors or in a well-ventilated place, away from the cooking flame and from guests. Check hoses for cracks and connections for leaks with soapy water before lighting: bubbles mean a leak. Never use a lighter to check for leaks. Light the match or lighter first, then open the gas. If you smell gas, turn off the cylinder valve, put out all flames, do not switch electrical items on or off, and move people away. Keep a fire extinguisher and a fire blanket at the cooking area.

blocks.title: Visit the venue first

lessons.title: Recipe costing with yield, food cost percentage and menu engineering
objectives: Convert as-purchased quantities to edible portions using yield percentage
Cost a standard recipe and set a price from a target food cost percentage
Classify menu items as stars, plowhorses, puzzles or dogs
Decide what to promote, reprice, redesign or remove from a menu

blocks.text: When you buy a whole chicken, a tuber of yam or a bunch of plantain, you do not serve all of it. Bones, peel, skin and trimmings are lost. Professional costing accounts for this with **yield**. Then it uses **food cost percentage** to set prices, and **menu engineering** to decide which dishes to push. These three tools go beyond simple cost-plus pricing and protect your profit on every order.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.caption: Yield, food cost percentage and menu analysis are the three calculations behind every profitable menu.

blocks.text: As purchased versus edible portion

**As purchased (AP)** is the weight you buy. **Edible portion (EP)** is the weight you can actually serve after trimming and cooking. **Yield percentage** = EP divided by AP x 100. You find it by testing, just as you tested cooking loss in Module 1. The true cost of the food you serve is the AP price divided by the yield.
These are illustrative test results. Your own figures will differ with produce size, season, supplier and cooking method, so test your main ingredients yourself and record them.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing and pricing a plate of fried yam and fish
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Asaba wants to add fried yam with peppered fish to her lunch menu. Her own tests give 80% yield for yam and 60% for fish. Prices are approximate.
steps: Portion: 200 g fried yam and 150 g fish (edible weight).
Yam: AP needed = 200 g divided by 0.80 = 250 g. At about N1,600 per kg, cost = 0.25 x 1,600 = N400.
Fish: AP needed = 150 g divided by 0.60 = 250 g. At about N4,000 per kg, cost = 0.25 x 4,000 = N1,000.
Pepper sauce, oil and seasoning from her standard recipes: N300. Total food cost per plate: N400 + N1,000 + N300 = N1,700.
Her target food cost is 35% of the selling price. Price = N1,700 divided by 0.35 = N4,857. She sets N5,000.
blocks.result: At N5,000, Chioma's food cost is 1,700 divided by 5,000 = 34%, within her target. The other 66% must cover packaging, gas, staff, rent, transport and profit.

blocks.title: Choosing a food cost target
blocks.text: Food cost percentage targets vary by business. Many restaurants work somewhere around 28% to 35%. A home caterer with low rent may accept a higher percentage; a business with paid staff and premises may need a lower one. Work out your own overheads before choosing.
Menu engineering

Menu engineering sorts dishes by two questions: how popular is it (how many sold) and how profitable is it (**contribution margin**, which is selling price minus food cost)? Compare each dish with the average of your menu.

blocks.title: The menu engineering matrix
items: Puzzle: promote it
Star: protect it
Dog: remove or redesign
Plowhorse: reprice or cut cost
blocks.caption: Each dish falls in one box, and each box suggests a different business decision.

items: **Star:** popular and high margin. Keep the quality and portion exactly the same and feature it.
**Plowhorse:** popular but low margin. Raise the price slightly, reduce a costly component, or pair it with a high-margin side.
**Puzzle:** high margin but rarely ordered. Rename it, photograph it better, recommend it on WhatsApp, or place it first on the menu.
**Dog:** unpopular and low margin. Remove it, or redesign it completely.

blocks.text: Repeat the analysis every month or two, because prices change quickly. When the cost of fish or oil jumps, a star can slide into the plowhorse box without you noticing. A simple notebook or spreadsheet with dish, number sold, price, food cost and margin is enough to keep watch.

blocks.title: Worked example: analysing a four-dish lunch menu
blocks.context: For example, Chioma reviews one month of sales on her lunch menu. Average sales per dish were 150 and average contribution margin was N3,000.
steps: Ofada rice with ayamase: 220 sold, margin N3,600. Above average on both: Star.
Rice and stew with chicken: 260 sold, margin N2,200. Popular but lower margin: Plowhorse.
Fried yam and peppered fish: 70 sold, margin N3,300. High margin, few sales: Puzzle.
Vegetable fried rice: 50 sold, margin N2,000. Below average on both: Dog.
blocks.result: Chioma keeps ofada as her signature, raises rice and chicken by N300, posts photos of the yam and fish on her WhatsApp status three times a week, and replaces the fried rice.

takeaways: Yield % = edible portion divided by as purchased x 100; test your own
Weight to buy = portion needed divided by yield
Price = food cost per plate divided by target food cost percentage
Contribution margin = selling price minus food cost
Menu engineering: protect stars, reprice plowhorses, promote puzzles, remove dogs

lessons.title: Compliance for food businesses: registration, NAFDAC, hygiene records and contracts
objectives: Identify which registrations and permits apply to a catering or food products business
Describe when NAFDAC registration is needed for packaged food
Keep the hygiene and traceability records an inspector or client expects
Protect yourself with a written client agreement

blocks.text: Being compliant does more than keep you out of trouble. Corporate clients, hotels, schools and supermarkets often ask for proof of registration and hygiene before they will buy from you. A tidy compliance pack can win you contracts that informal competitors cannot bid for. This lesson gives you an overview; always check current requirements with the agencies themselves, because rules and fees change.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.caption: Registration and records turn a home kitchen into a business that larger clients can trust.

blocks.text: Who regulates what

head: Requirement
Who handles it
When it applies
rows: Before trading under a business name, opening a business bank account or bidding for contracts
Tax authorities; often issued alongside CAC registration
For business banking, contracts and invoices to companies
Before selling pre-packaged food such as spice blends, sauces or dried products in shops and markets
Premises hygiene and food handler fitness
State and local government environmental health and health authorities
Rules vary by state; ask your local government environmental health office

blocks.text: For CAC, register through the official CAC online portal or an accredited agent, and do not pay anyone who promises registration without an official payment receipt. A registered business name must file annual returns every year, so add that date to your calendar.
NAFDAC and packaged products

NAFDAC (the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) regulates food that is processed, packaged and sold. Freshly cooked food served at an event is usually handled by state and local health authorities rather than product registration, but the moment you package a spice blend, pepper sauce or dried product for sale on shelves, NAFDAC registration applies. NAFDAC has guidance for small-scale producers. The process generally includes a premises inspection, documents and product samples for laboratory analysis. Get current requirements and fees from NAFDAC's official website or nearest office, not from social media agents.
Hygiene and traceability records

items: **Supplier list:** where you buy each main ingredient, with phone numbers.
**Batch or event record:** date, menu, quantities, who cooked, and for products a batch number on every pack.
**Temperature log:** fridge and freezer readings daily; hot-holding and reheating checks at events.
**Cleaning schedule:** what is cleaned, how often and by whom, signed off.
**Pest control:** dates of checks and treatments by a licensed provider; no poisons near food.
**Staff hygiene:** training dates, and a rule that anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or infected cuts does not handle food.
**Complaints log:** what was reported, what you checked and what you changed.

blocks.text: Records do not need to be complicated. A hardback notebook kept in the kitchen, or a shared Google Sheet updated from your phone, works well. The important thing is that entries are made at the time, not filled in later from memory, and that you keep them for a set period, such as at least a year.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a complaint
blocks.context: For example, a client calls Sade in Ilorin to say two guests felt unwell after a party she catered on Saturday.
steps: Sade thanks the client, takes details calmly, and advises that anyone unwell should see a health worker. She does not argue or admit fault on the phone.
She opens Saturday's event record: menu, cooking times, who cooked, and the hot-holding log showing stew at 68 C to 75 C during service.
She checks her supplier list for that week's chicken and her retained sample of each dish, kept chilled for 72 hours after the event as her own policy.
She notes that the coleslaw was held in a cooler, but no temperature was recorded for it, and adds a cold-holding check to her procedure.
She writes everything in the complaints log and follows up with the client in writing within 24 hours.
blocks.result: Because Sade kept records, she can answer factual questions, cooperate with health authorities if they investigate, and fix the one gap she found.

blocks.title: Your food business compliance pack
items: CAC certificate and TIN
NAFDAC numbers for products
Local health permits as required
Hygiene and temperature records
Signed client agreements
blocks.caption: Keep paper and phone copies together so you can show them to any client or inspector.

blocks.title: Write it down with clients
blocks.text: Before every event, send a short written agreement: menu, guest numbers, service style, price, deposit and balance dates, what happens if guest numbers change, cancellation terms, what the client provides (venue kitchen, water, power) and the time you hand over. Keep payments in your business account.

blocks.title: Honest claims only
blocks.text: Do not print or post health claims such as "cures diabetes" or "boosts fertility" for any food or spice blend. Such claims can mislead customers and break advertising and NAFDAC rules.

takeaways: Register with CAC and keep annual returns up to date
Packaged foods for sale need NAFDAC registration; get requirements from NAFDAC directly
Local and state authorities handle premises hygiene and food handler rules
Records of suppliers, temperatures, cleaning and complaints protect you and your clients
Use written client agreements and never make health claims

quiz.q: Patience is serving a staffed buffet to 200 guests. Using one line per 75 to 100 guests, how many buffet lines should she plan?
quiz.explain: 200 divided by 100 = 2, and 200 divided by 75 = 2.7. So 2 to 3 lines, served from both sides where possible.

quiz.q: At a venue, Ireti smells gas near the cylinder. What should she do first?
options: Light a match to find the leak
Turn off the cylinder valve and put out all flames
Switch on a fan to clear the smell
Carry on cooking and check later
quiz.explain: Shut off the gas and remove ignition sources first. Never use a flame to find a leak, and do not switch electrical items on or off.

quiz.q: Plantain has a 65% yield. How much unpeeled plantain must Chioma buy for 50 portions of 130 g peeled plantain?
quiz.explain: 50 x 130 g = 6,500 g edible. 6,500 divided by 0.65 = 10,000 g, so about 10 kg.

quiz.q: A dish costs N1,400 in food. Chioma's target food cost is 35%. What price should she set at minimum?
quiz.explain: Price = 1,400 divided by 0.35 = N4,000.

quiz.q: A dish sells very well but has a low contribution margin. In menu engineering it is a:
quiz.explain: Popular with low margin is a plowhorse. Consider a small price rise or reducing a costly component.

quiz.q: Bimpe wants to sell her bottled pepper sauce in supermarkets. Which agency must register the product?
quiz.explain: NAFDAC registers processed, packaged food sold to the public. CAC registers the business itself.

finalQuiz.q: Why should stock start in cold water and never be salted?
options: Cold water makes it boil faster, and salt causes foam
Proteins rise slowly as skimmable foam, and salt becomes too strong after reduction
Cold water removes gelatin, and salt prevents clouding
It saves gas, and salt spoils stock
finalQuiz.explain: Starting cold lets proteins rise as foam you can skim. Stock is often reduced, so any salt would concentrate.

finalQuiz.q: Grilled chicken quarters lose 25% of their weight. How much raw chicken is needed for 60 portions of 150 g cooked?
finalQuiz.explain: 60 x 150 g = 9,000 g cooked. 9,000 divided by 0.75 = 12,000 g, so 12 kg raw.

finalQuiz.q: Frying oil is dark, foams heavily and smokes at normal heat. What should Funke do?
options: Add fresh oil and keep using it
Strain it and use it once more
Heat it higher to burn off the foam
finalQuiz.explain: Dark colour, heavy foaming and smoking at normal heat all mean the oil has broken down.

finalQuiz.q: Ngozi's blended stew mix weighs 6 kg and she wants to halve it before frying. What should it weigh after boiling down?
finalQuiz.explain: Halving 6 kg leaves 3 kg. Boiling off water first gives a sweeter, cleaner stew that fries quickly.

finalQuiz.q: Which combination gives better quality protein for a family on a tight budget?
finalQuiz.explain: Cereals and legumes complement each other's amino acids, so rice and beans together give better protein.

finalQuiz.q: A woman weighs 60 kg. About how much protein does she need daily at 0.83 g per kg?
finalQuiz.explain: 60 x 0.83 = 49.8 g, so about 50 g a day.

finalQuiz.q: Which change best helps a child absorb iron from a bean meal?
options: Serve it with an orange or pawpaw
finalQuiz.explain: Vitamin C eaten with the meal improves absorption of plant iron. Tea reduces it.

finalQuiz.q: WHO advises adults to eat less than how much salt a day?
finalQuiz.explain: Less than 5 g a day, just under one level teaspoon, including salt from seasoning cubes and processed foods.

finalQuiz.q: Zainab dries 20 kg of tomatoes (about 94% water) to 10% moisture. About how much dried tomato will she get?
finalQuiz.explain: Dry matter = 6% of 20 kg = 1.2 kg. 1.2 divided by 0.90 = about 1.33 kg.

finalQuiz.q: Hadiza's yaji formula is 55% kuli kuli powder. How much kuli kuli does she need for an 8 kg batch?
A plate's food cost is N2,100 and Chioma's target food cost is 30%. What selling price meets the target?
Which item belongs in a food business compliance pack?
finalQuiz.explain: Temperature logs and cleaning records show hygiene control to clients and inspectors. Customer data must be kept private.
